passages.title: Chorsu Bazaar
passages.text:
Chorsu Bazaar is one of the oldest markets in Tashkent. It is in the old part of the city, under a large blue dome. Every day, thousands of people come here to buy fruit, vegetables, bread, spices and meat.

The market opens early in the morning, at about five o'clock, because many sellers bring fresh food from villages near the city. Prices are usually lower than in supermarkets, and buyers often ask for a discount.

Tourists like Chorsu too. They take photos of the colourful spices and try fresh bread called non. Some visitors say the best time to come is in the morning, when the market is not too crowded and the food is freshest.

questions.q: Chorsu Bazaar is in the new part of Tashkent.
The market opens at about five in the morning.
Food at Chorsu is usually cheaper than in supermarkets.
Why does the market open early?
options: Sellers bring fresh food from villages
It is too hot later in the day

questions.q: Chorsu is the biggest market in Uzbekistan.

passages.title: Learning languages with apps
passages.text:
In the last ten years, millions of people have started learning languages on their phones. Language apps are popular because they are cheap or free, and learners can practise for a few minutes at any time — on the bus, in a queue or before going to sleep. Many apps turn learning into a game: users earn points, compete with friends and receive reminders if they forget to practise.

However, teachers point out that apps have limits. Most of them focus on single words and short sentences, so learners get little practice in writing longer texts or having real conversations. A study at a university in Spain found that students who used an app for three months knew more words than before, but their speaking had hardly improved.

For this reason, many teachers suggest using apps together with lessons, not instead of them.

questions.q: Language apps can be used at any time of day.
All language apps are free.
According to teachers, apps give learners a lot of practice in writing long texts.
What did the study in Spain find?
options: The students' speaking improved a lot
The students learned more words, but their speaking barely changed
The students stopped using the app after three months

questions.q: The students in the Spanish study used the app every day.

passages.title: Urban heat islands
passages.text:
On a summer afternoon, the centre of a large city can be several degrees hotter than the countryside around it. Scientists call this the urban heat island effect. It occurs mainly because roads, roofs and pavements absorb the sun's energy during the day and release it slowly at night, so cities stay warm long after sunset. The lack of vegetation makes matters worse: trees and plants cool the air by releasing water through their leaves, and they also provide shade. Heat from cars, air conditioners and factories adds to the problem.

The consequences are more than a matter of comfort. Higher temperatures increase the demand for air conditioning, which raises electricity consumption and, in turn, produces more heat. During heatwaves, hospitals in hot cities report more cases of heat-related illness, particularly among elderly people.

Several cities have started to fight back. Some paint roofs white so that they reflect sunlight, while others plant thousands of trees along their streets. Early results are encouraging, although experts warn that the benefits depend on how carefully such measures are planned.

questions.q: Cities cool down quickly after the sun goes down.
Plants help to lower the temperature of the air.
Which group is mentioned as especially affected by heatwaves?
Using air conditioners can make the heat island effect stronger.
Painting roofs white costs less than planting trees.

passages.title: The value of boredom
passages.text:
For most of history, boredom has been regarded as something to be avoided — a sign of a dull mind or an empty life. Recently, however, psychologists have begun to take a more nuanced view. In one widely cited experiment, participants were first asked to complete a deliberately tedious task, such as copying numbers from a telephone directory, and were then asked to think of as many uses as possible for a pair of plastic cups. Those who had endured the boring task produced more ideas, and more original ones, than a control group who had gone straight to the creative exercise.

The researchers' explanation is that boredom prompts the mind to wander, and that daydreaming allows connections to form between ideas that would not normally be linked. Critics caution against over-interpreting such findings: the studies have mostly involved small groups of university students, and it is not clear whether the effect lasts beyond a few minutes.

Nonetheless, some educators argue that the constant stimulation provided by smartphones may be depriving young people of the mental idleness from which creativity often springs.

questions.q: Psychologists have always considered boredom to be useful.
In the experiment, the group that did the boring task first gave more original answers.
The researchers believe daydreaming helps people link ideas that are usually unconnected.
What concern do critics raise?
options: The tasks were too difficult for the participants
The evidence comes from limited groups, and the effect may be short-lived
The control group was larger than the other group

questions.q: Participants in the experiment were paid for taking part.

passages.title: Language death
passages.text:
Of the roughly seven thousand languages spoken today, linguists estimate that as many as half may cease to be spoken by the end of this century. Language death is seldom abrupt. More often, it proceeds through a gradual shift in which a community comes to use a more dominant language in an ever-widening range of situations — first at work and in school, eventually in the home — until parents no longer pass the ancestral tongue on to their children. At that point the language may linger among elderly speakers for decades, but its fate is effectively sealed.

The loss is not merely symbolic. Each language encodes distinctive ways of categorising experience, and many contain detailed knowledge of local plants, animals and ecosystems that has never been recorded elsewhere. Yet attempts at revitalisation have had mixed results. Hebrew is frequently cited as a success, having been revived as an everyday spoken language after centuries of use confined largely to religious and scholarly contexts; such cases, however, depended on exceptional political and social circumstances that are rarely replicated.

Where revival efforts rely chiefly on school lessons, students may acquire a passive understanding without ever adopting the language for daily communication — an outcome that some linguists regard as preservation rather than revival.

questions.q: Most languages disappear suddenly.
A language is likely to die once parents stop passing it on to their children.
Some languages hold knowledge about nature that has not been written down in any other form.
Why is Hebrew described as an unusual case?
options: It was never used in religious contexts
Its revival depended on rare political and social conditions
It was revived mainly through school lessons

questions.q: What does the writer suggest about revival programmes based on school lessons?
options: They usually produce fluent everyday speakers
They may keep a language understood but not truly in use
They are more successful than political campaigns
